items.prompt: What tells a tree that autumn is on the way?

options.label: The first frost
options.feedback: Frost arrives too late. A tree caught unprepared by frost would lose its leaves still full of goodness.

options.label: The days getting shorter
options.feedback: The one signal that arrives at the same date every year, whatever the weather.

options.label: The soil drying out
options.feedback: Soil dries in high summer too, and a tree does not shed its leaves in July.

options.label: The wind turning colder
options.feedback: Cold snaps come and go all year. A tree that trusted them would strip itself in a chilly August.

items.ok_line: Weather lies; the length of the day never does.
items.ko_line: Preparing for winter takes weeks. The signal has to come before the cold, not with it.
items.exp_title: The one signal that never lies
items.exp_text: Weather is a poor calendar: a warm October and a cold August both happen, and a tree that trusted temperature would be caught out. Day length is fixed by the tilt of the Earth and repeats to the hour every year. So a tree measures the shortening of the day, and begins emptying its leaves weeks before the first frost.

items.prompt: What does a plant actually measure to know how long the day is?

options.label: The total light it received
options.feedback: A cloudy long day would then count as a bright short one, and the plant would be fooled every overcast week.

options.label: The highest point the sun reached
options.feedback: Nothing in a leaf tracks the angle of the sun. And clouds would hide it for days on end.

options.label: The length of unbroken darkness
options.feedback: It is the night that is timed, and a single flash of light in the middle of it resets the count.

options.label: The warmth of the afternoon
options.feedback: That is temperature again, and temperature is exactly the unreliable signal a plant is avoiding.

items.ok_line: The dark is what gets counted.
items.ko_line: Day and night add up to the same total. A plant only needs to time one of them — and it picked the quieter one.
items.exp_title: Counting the dark, not the light
items.exp_text: A leaf holds a substance that is changed by light and slowly changes back in darkness. The longer the night runs undisturbed, the further back it drifts, and where it has got to by morning is the plant's reading of the season. So what the plant measures is not the day at all but the unbroken length of the night.

items.prompt: Where do the yellows and oranges of an autumn leaf come from?

options.label: They were always there, hidden under the green
options.feedback: Uncovered rather than made. Green was simply louder all summer.

options.label: The leaf makes them as it dies
options.feedback: A dying leaf is dismantling itself, not starting new work.

options.label: The cold turns the green pigment yellow
options.feedback: Chlorophyll is not converted. It is taken apart and carried away.

options.label: Dust and dirt settling on the leaf
options.feedback: The colour is inside the leaf, and it is far too even and too bright to be dirt.

items.ok_line: The colour was under the green all along.
items.ko_line: Ask whether something is being added, or something is being taken away.
items.exp_title: What is left when the green goes
items.exp_text: Chlorophyll is expensive, and a tree will not throw it away with the leaf. Through autumn it is broken down and the useful parts are drawn back into the branches for the spring. The yellow and orange pigments that worked alongside it all summer are not withdrawn, and with the green gone they are simply what remains to be seen.

items.prompt: Why does a tree drop its leaves for the winter at all?

options.label: The leaves would freeze and burst
options.feedback: Frost does damage a soft leaf, but a tree sheds long before the hardest frosts and evergreens keep theirs through worse.

options.label: To let more light reach the ground
options.feedback: The tree gains nothing by lighting the ground beneath it, and in winter there is little light to share.

options.label: Leaves lose water the frozen ground cannot replace
options.feedback: A leaf leaks water all day, and a root in frozen soil can draw none.

options.label: The wind would blow the tree over
options.feedback: A bare tree does catch less wind, which helps, but that is a bonus rather than the reason.

items.ok_line: Winter is a drought as much as a freeze.
items.ko_line: A leaf is always leaking. Ask where the replacement comes from when the ground is solid.
items.exp_text: Every open pore on a leaf loses water, and in summer the roots simply send up more. When the soil freezes, the roots can draw nothing, and a tree in full leaf would dry out while standing in ice. Shedding removes the leaks, and the tree waits out the winter closed.

items.prompt: What does a bud need before it will open in spring?

options.label: Only one warm day
options.feedback: Warm days happen in January. A bud that opened on the first of them would lose everything to the next frost.

options.label: A long spell of cold, then lengthening days
options.feedback: The cold has to be counted first, which is what stops a bud opening in a mild winter week.

options.label: Heavy rain
options.feedback: Rain matters to a tree, but a bud will sit closed through the wettest winter.

options.label: Its old leaves to rot away
options.feedback: The leaves fell months earlier, and evergreens open buds with all their leaves still on.

items.ok_line: Cold first, then light. Both, or nothing.
items.ko_line: A single warm week in winter opens nothing. Ask what is missing.
items.exp_text: A bud formed in summer is held shut, and warmth alone will not release it. It first has to sit through a long run of cold, which it counts; only once that count is filled does the bud start answering to warmth and lengthening days. That is why a mild spell in midwinter passes without a single bud opening, and why the same warmth in March throws the whole tree into leaf.

items.prompt: What starts a bird preparing to migrate?

options.label: Running out of food
options.feedback: Many birds leave while food is still plentiful. Waiting for hunger would leave them too weak to fly.

options.label: The first cold night
options.feedback: Departure would then vary by weeks from one year to the next, and the whole flock would scatter.

options.label: The changing length of the day
options.feedback: Weeks ahead of any shortage, the day length shifts the bird's body into travelling condition.

options.label: Watching other birds leave
options.feedback: Young birds raised alone still get restless at the right season and set off in the right direction.

items.ok_line: It leaves before it has any reason to be hungry.
items.ko_line: Fattening up for a long flight takes weeks. Ask what could give that much warning.
items.exp_text: Crossing a sea or a desert takes fuel, and a bird has to lay it on in advance. Shortening days act on the bird's body weeks early: it feeds harder, lays down fat, and grows restless at night even when kept from flying. So the signal that starts the journey is the length of the day, arriving long before the cold or the hunger it prepares for.

items.prompt: Why is day length a better seasonal signal than temperature?

options.label: It repeats exactly the same way every year
options.feedback: Same date, same length, always. Nothing else about the year is that dependable.

options.label: It is easier for a living thing to sense
options.feedback: Sensing warmth is if anything simpler. Reliability is what settles it, not ease.

options.label: It changes more quickly
options.feedback: Temperature can swing more in a day than day length does in a month. Speed is not the point.

options.label: It works underwater as well
options.feedback: Light does reach into water, but so does warmth. Neither is ruled out.

items.ok_line: You can build a life around something that never varies.
items.ko_line: Both signals can be sensed. The question is which one tells the truth every year.
items.exp_text: Temperature wanders. A warm February and a cold May both happen, and a creature that acted on warmth would breed or bud at the wrong moment in those years and lose everything. Day length is set by the tilt of the Earth and cannot wander, so the fifteenth of March is the same length of day whatever the sky is doing — and that is why living things set their year by it.

items.prompt: What makes a stoat or a ptarmigan turn white for the winter?

options.label: The snow reflecting onto its coat
options.feedback: The change begins before the snow falls, which is the whole point of it.

options.label: Cold bleaching the fur
options.feedback: Cold does not bleach hair. The white coat is grown, and grown deliberately.

options.label: The shortening days
options.feedback: The animal starts changing before the snow, so as to be white when it comes.

options.label: Eating different food
options.feedback: Diet can tint some animals, like a flamingo, but it plays no part in this change.

items.ok_line: White before the snow, not after it.
items.ko_line: Growing a whole new coat takes weeks. Ask what could give the warning in time.
items.exp_text: A brown animal on snow is visible from a long way off, and so is a white one on bare ground — the coat has to change at the right moment or it is worse than useless. Growing it takes weeks, so the animal cannot wait for the snow. Shortening days set the moult going in advance, and the animal is white by the time the ground is.

items.prompt: Why do many animals near the equator breed all year round?

options.label: There are no predators there
options.feedback: The tropics are full of predators. If anything the pressure is greater.

options.label: The day length barely changes
options.feedback: With no shifting signal, there is no season to wait for.

options.label: It is too hot to raise young quickly
options.feedback: Heat does not slow the raising of young, and breeding all year is a sign of ease rather than difficulty.

options.label: Their young grow up faster
options.feedback: Some do and some do not, and it has no bearing on when the breeding starts.

items.ko_line: The seasonal signal is the same everywhere. Ask how much of it reaches the equator.
items.exp_text: At the equator the sun rises and sets at nearly the same hour in every month of the year. The signal that tells animals elsewhere when to breed is therefore almost flat there, and there is no cold season to survive and no short one to squeeze the young into. Breeding is spread through the whole year instead of packed into a spring.

options.label: One that lives for a long time
options.feedback: That is a perennial, and it has nothing to do with the length of a day.

options.label: One that takes all day to open its flowers
options.feedback: How fast a flower opens is a matter of hours. The name is about the season, not the morning.

options.label: One that needs long days to grow tall
options.feedback: Every plant grows more in long days. The name marks when it flowers, not how it grows.

options.label: One that flowers only when nights are short
options.feedback: Named for the day, but triggered by the night, as always with these plants.

items.ok_line: Triggered by the night, all the same.
items.ko_line: The name marks the one moment in the year the plant is waiting for.
items.exp_title: A name that points the wrong way
items.exp_text: A long-day plant flowers as the days lengthen towards midsummer, and a short-day plant waits for them to draw in towards autumn. But what either one is really timing is the dark between: the long-day plant flowers once the night has fallen below a certain length. The name says day because that is what we notice, and the plant is counting the other half.
